e-612.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function
e-612.problem: Find $\mathbf F(t)$ given that $\mathbf F'(t)= \langle 6t^5+2t, \sec^2 t\rangle.$
e-612.worked_solution:
Note that 

$$
\mathbf F(t)=\int \mathbf F'(t)\, \textrm d t=\int \left\langle 6t^5+2t,\, \sec^2 t\right\rangle \, \textrm d t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨6{t}^{5}+2t,\,{sec}^{2}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int (6{t}^{5}+2t)\,\text{d}t,\,\int {sec}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{6}+{t}^{2}+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{6}+{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{6}+{t}^{2},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $\mathbf C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

e-613.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1),\,4⟩\,\text{d}t=⟨\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1)\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t) =\cos(2t+1),$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u= 2t +1.$ Then

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d t} = 2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm d t = \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡u)+{c}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1)+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t) =4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t=\int 4\text{d}t=4t+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+1),\,4⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1)+{c}_{1},\,4t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1),\,4t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t+1),\,4t⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

e-615.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function That Satisfies a Given Initial Condition
e-615.problem: Calculate $\mathbf F(t)$ given that $\mathbf F'(t)= \left\langle \sec t \tan t, \,  \sin(2t)\right\rangle$ and $\mathbf F(0)=\langle 0,\, 0\rangle.$
e-615.worked_solution:
Note that 

$$
\mathbf F(t)=\int \mathbf F'(t)\, \textrm d t=\int \left\langle \sec t \tan t,\,  \sin(2t)\right\rangle \, \textrm d t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int \operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $\mathbf F(0)=\left\langle 0,\, 0 \right\rangle$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0)=⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡0+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\cdot 0)+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨1+{c}_{1},\,-\frac{1}{2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨0,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $c_1=-1$ and $c_2=\dfrac 12.$ Consequently, 

$$
\mathbf F(t)=\left\langle  \sec t - 1  , \,  -\dfrac 1 2\cos(2t)+ \dfrac12\right\rangle.
$$

after.worked_solution:

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨{e}^{t}-4,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t.

$$

$$

after.html:
Question 1
?

If F′(t)=⟨et−4,sin⁡t⟩, then F(t)=

a
−⟨et−4t,cos⁡t⟩+C
b
⟨et,−cos⁡t⟩+C
c
⟨et−4t,−cos⁡t⟩+C
d
⟨et−4t,cos⁡t⟩+C
e
⟨et−4t,sin⁡t⟩+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨et−4,sin⁡t⟩dt.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

∫⟨et−4,sin⁡t⟩dt=⟨∫(et−4)dt,∫sin⁡tdt⟩=⟨et−4t+c1,−cos⁡t+c2⟩=⟨et−4t,−cos⁡t⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨et−4t,−cos⁡t⟩+C,

where C is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option c. Integrating componentwise gives e^t−4t and −cos(t); differentiating these returns e^t−4 and sin(t). Option d has the wrong sign on the cosine term.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨{e}^{t}-4,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t}-4,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int ({e}^{t}-4)\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}-4t+{c}_{1},\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}-4t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}-4t,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

before.html:
Question 2
?

If F′(t)=⟨5t4,−1t2⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨t5,1t⟩+C
b
⟨t5,−1t⟩+C
c
⟨4t4,1t⟩+C
d
⟨t4,−1t⟩+C
e
⟨t4,3t3⟩+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating componentwise, ∫5t^4 dt = t^5 and ∫−t^(−2) dt = t^(−1) = 1/t. Thus F(t) = ⟨t^5, 1/t⟩ + C, which is option a.

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\text{ }5{t}^{4},\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨5{t}^{4},\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int 5{t}^{4}\,\text{d}t,\int (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{5}+{c}_{1},\,\frac{1}{t}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{5},\,\frac{1}{t}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{5},\,\frac{1}{t}⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

Question 2
?

If F′(t)=⟨5t4,−1t2⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨t5,1t⟩+C
b
⟨t5,−1t⟩+C
c
⟨4t4,1t⟩+C
d
⟨t4,−1t⟩+C
e
⟨t4,3t3⟩+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨ 5t4,−1t2⟩dt.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

∫⟨5t4,−1t2⟩dt=⟨∫5t4dt,∫(−1t2)dt⟩=⟨t5+c1,1t+c2⟩=⟨t5,1t⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨t5,1t⟩+C,

where C is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\text{ }5{t}^{4},\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨5{t}^{4},\,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int 5{t}^{4}\,\text{d}t,\int (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{5}+{c}_{1},\,\frac{1}{t}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{5},\,\frac{1}{t}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{5},\,\frac{1}{t}⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

decision.explanation: Integrate each component: ∫3t² dt = t³ and ∫e^t dt = e^t. Adding an arbitrary constant vector gives option c.

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨3{t}^{2},\,{e}^{t}⟩\,\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨3{t}^{2},\,{e}^{t}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int 3{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t,\,\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}+{c}_{1},\,{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3},\,{e}^{t}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3},\,{e}^{t}⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

Question 3
?

If F′(t)=⟨3t2,et⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨t3,−et⟩+C
b
⟨t33,et⟩+C
c
⟨t3,et⟩+C
d
⟨t3,−tet⟩+C
e
⟨3t3,tet⟩+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨3t2,et⟩dt.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

∫⟨3t2,et⟩dt=⟨∫3t2dt,∫etdt⟩=⟨t3+c1,et+c2⟩=⟨t3,et⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨t3,et⟩+C,

where C is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option c: integrating 3t² gives t³, and integrating e^t gives e^t. Differentiating ⟨t³, e^t⟩ + C recovers the given derivative. Option a has an incorrect negative sign.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨3{t}^{2},\,{e}^{t}⟩\,\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨3{t}^{2},\,{e}^{t}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int 3{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t,\,\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3}+{c}_{1},\,{e}^{t}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3},\,{e}^{t}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{t}^{3},\,{e}^{t}⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

Question 4

If F′(t)=⟨sec⁡ttan⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨−csc⁡t,cos⁡t⟩+C
b
⟨sec⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩+C
c
⟨sec⁡ttan⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩+C
d
⟨sec⁡t,cos⁡t⟩+C
e
⟨csc⁡t,cos⁡t⟩+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrate componentwise: the derivative of sec(t) is sec(t)tan(t), and the derivative of cos(t) is −sin(t). Therefore option d gives the required antiderivative.

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int \operatorname{sec}⁡t\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,\text{d}t,-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sec}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

If F′(t)=⟨sec⁡ttan⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨−csc⁡t,cos⁡t⟩+C
b
⟨sec⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩+C
c
⟨sec⁡ttan⁡t,−cos⁡t⟩+C
d
⟨sec⁡t,cos⁡t⟩+C
e
⟨csc⁡t,cos⁡t⟩+C
Submit
Correct

First, we note that F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨sec⁡ttan⁡t,−sin⁡t⟩dt.

where C is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

before.html:
Question 5
?

If F′(t)=⟨6t3+8,et+1⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨3t4+8t,et+1⟩+C
b
⟨t42+8t,et+1⟩+C
c
⟨3t42+8t,et−1⟩+C
d
⟨3t42+8t,et+1⟩+C
e
⟨4t23,et⟩+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating componentwise gives ∫(6t³+8) dt = 3t⁴/2+8t and ∫e^(t+1) dt = e^(t+1). Adding a constant vector gives option d.

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨6{t}^{3}+8,\,{e}^{t+1}⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨6{t}^{3}+8,\,{e}^{t+1}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int (6{t}^{3}+8)\,\text{d}t,\int {e}^{t+1}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3{t}^{4}}{2}+8t+{c}_{1},\,{e}^{t+1}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3{t}^{4}}{2}+8t,\,{e}^{t+1}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3{t}^{4}}{2}+8t,\,{e}^{t+1}⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

Question 5
?

If F′(t)=⟨6t3+8,et+1⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨3t4+8t,et+1⟩+C
b
⟨t42+8t,et+1⟩+C
c
⟨3t42+8t,et−1⟩+C
d
⟨3t42+8t,et+1⟩+C
e
⟨4t23,et⟩+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨6t3+8,et+1⟩dt.

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

∫⟨6t3+8,et+1⟩dt=⟨∫(6t3+8)dt,∫et+1dt⟩=⟨3t42+8t+c1,et+1+c2⟩=⟨3t42+8t,et+1⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨3t42+8t,et+1⟩+C,

where C is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨6{t}^{3}+8,\,{e}^{t+1}⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨6{t}^{3}+8,\,{e}^{t+1}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int (6{t}^{3}+8)\,\text{d}t,\int {e}^{t+1}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3{t}^{4}}{2}+8t+{c}_{1},\,{e}^{t+1}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3{t}^{4}}{2}+8t,\,{e}^{t+1}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3{t}^{4}}{2}+8t,\,{e}^{t+1}⟩+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary (vector) constant of integration.

before.html:
Question 6
?

Find ∫⟨4csc2⁡t,3e3t⟩dt.

a
⟨sin2⁡t,e3t⟩+C
b
⟨−4cos⁡t,e3t⟩+C
c
⟨4tan⁡t,3e3t⟩+C
d
⟨−4cot⁡t,e3t⟩+C
e
⟨−4cot⁡t,3e3t⟩+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrate each component: ∫4csc²(t) dt = −4cot(t), and ∫3e^(3t) dt = e^(3t). Adding an arbitrary constant vector gives option d.

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨4{csc}^{2}⁡t,\,3{e}^{3t}⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int 4{csc}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t,\,\int 3{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-4\operatorname{cot}⁡t+{c}_{1},\,{e}^{3t}+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-4\operatorname{cot}⁡t,\,{e}^{3t}⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-4\operatorname{cot}⁡t,\,{e}^{3t}⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 7
after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩\text{d}t=⟨\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)={e}^{t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t}\text{d}t={e}^{t}+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u=2t.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 4\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =2(-\operatorname{cos}⁡u)+{c}_{2} \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩\text{d}t & =⟨{e}^{t}+{c}_{1},\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Find ∫⟨et,4sin⁡2t⟩dt.

a
⟨tet,−2cos⁡2t⟩+C
b
⟨e,2+cos⁡2t⟩+C
c
⟨et,−2sin⁡2t⟩+C
d
⟨et,−2cos⁡2t⟩+C
e
⟨et,2−cos⁡2t⟩+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

∫⟨et,4sin⁡2t⟩dt=⟨∫etdt,∫4sin⁡2tdt⟩.

  • For x(t)=et, we have ∫x(t)dt=∫etdt=et+c1.

  • For y(t)=4sin⁡2t, we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let u=2t. Then
    dudt=2⟹dt=12du. Therefore, we have ∫y(t)dt=∫4sin⁡2tdt=∫4sin⁡u⋅12du=42∫sin⁡udu=2(−cos⁡u)+c2=−2cos⁡2t+c2.

Finally, we get

∫⟨et,4sin⁡2t⟩dt=⟨et+c1,−2cos⁡2t+c2⟩=⟨et,−2cos⁡2t⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨et,−2cos⁡2t⟩+C.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option d. Componentwise integration gives e^t and −2cos(2t); differentiating −2cos(2t) yields 4sin(2t). Option e instead yields only 2sin(2t) in its second component.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩\text{d}t=⟨\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int 4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $x(t)={e}^{t},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x(t)\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{t}\text{d}t={e}^{t}+{c}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For $y(t)=4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,$ we calculate its integral using substitution. So, we let $u=2t.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2\,⟹\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,  we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int 4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int 4\operatorname{sin}⁡u\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =2(-\operatorname{cos}⁡u)+{c}_{2} \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+{c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t⟩\text{d}t & =⟨{e}^{t}+{c}_{1},\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,-2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Find ∫⟨et,cos⁡t⟩dt.

a
⟨2et,−sin⁡t⟩+C
b
⟨et,cos⁡t⟩+C
c
⟨et,sin⁡t⟩+C
d
⟨2e2t,−cos⁡t⟩+C
e
⟨12et,sin⁡t⟩+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrate each component separately: ∫e^t dt = e^t and ∫cos(t) dt = sin(t). Adding an arbitrary constant vector gives option c.

after.name: Question 8
after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

∫⟨et,cos⁡t⟩dt=⟨∫etdt,∫cos⁡tdt⟩=⟨et+c1,sin⁡t+c2⟩=⟨et,sin⁡t⟩+⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨et,sin⁡t⟩+C.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{t},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t,\,\int \operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t}+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{t},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩+C.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option e. The derivative of −e^(−t) is e^(−t), and the derivative of sec(t) is tan(t)sec(t). Option c instead has second-component derivative sec²(t).

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨{e}^{-t},\operatorname{tan}⁡t\operatorname{sec}⁡t⟩\,\text{d}t & =⟨\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t,\int \operatorname{tan}⁡t\operatorname{sec}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-{e}^{-t}+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{sec}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-{e}^{-t},\,\operatorname{sec}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-{e}^{-t},\,\operatorname{sec}⁡t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

a

b

c

decision.explanation: Integrate componentwise: ∫t^(−2) dt = −1/t, and the derivative of csc(t) is −cot(t)csc(t). Therefore the antiderivative is option a.

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},\,-\operatorname{cot}⁡t\operatorname{csc}⁡t⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int \frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t,\,\int -\operatorname{cot}⁡t\operatorname{csc}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{t}+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{csc}⁡t+{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{t},\,\operatorname{csc}⁡t⟩+⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{t},\,\operatorname{csc}⁡t⟩+C\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Evaluate componentwise: √2[sin(t)] from 0 to π/4 = √2·(√2/2) = 1, and [tan(t)] from 0 to π/4 = 1−0 = 1. Thus option e is correct.

after.name: Question 14
after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each componentt separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}⟨\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{sec}^{2}⁡t⟩\text{d}t & =⟨{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t,{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sec}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t\,\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4}⟩ \\  & =⟨\text{ }\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi /4)-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0),\,\operatorname{tan}⁡(\pi /4)-\operatorname{tan}⁡(0)⟩ \\  & =⟨\text{ }\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}-0,\,1-0⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Integrate componentwise: [(2/5)√t] from 1 to 16 = (2/5)(4−1) = 6/5. [(2/3)(t−1)^(3/2)] from 1 to 16 = (2/3)·15√15 = 10√15. Thus option d is correct.

after.name: Question 15
after.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{16}⟨\frac{1}{5\sqrt{t}},\,\sqrt{t-1}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨{\int }_{1}^{16}\frac{1}{5\sqrt{t}}\,\text{d}t,{\int }_{1}^{16}\sqrt{t-1}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{5}\sqrt{t}\,\,{|}_{1}^{16},\,\frac{2\sqrt{(t-1)^{3}}}{3}\,\,{|}_{1}^{16}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{5}\cdot \sqrt{16}-\frac{2}{5}\cdot \sqrt{1},\,\frac{2\sqrt{(16-1)^{3}}}{3}-\frac{2\sqrt{(1-1)^{3}}}{3}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{6}{5},\,10\sqrt{15}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Definite Integral of a Vector-Valued Function
content.worked_solution:
To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{16}⟨\frac{1}{5\sqrt{t}},\,\sqrt{t-1}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨{\int }_{1}^{16}\frac{1}{5\sqrt{t}}\,\text{d}t,{\int }_{1}^{16}\sqrt{t-1}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{5}\sqrt{t}\,\,{|}_{1}^{16},\,\frac{2\sqrt{(t-1)^{3}}}{3}\,\,{|}_{1}^{16}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{5}\cdot \sqrt{16}-\frac{2}{5}\cdot \sqrt{1},\,\frac{2\sqrt{(16-1)^{3}}}{3}-\frac{2\sqrt{(1-1)^{3}}}{3}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{6}{5},\,10\sqrt{15}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Integrating componentwise gives F(t) = ⟨(t−1)³+c₁, t⁴−t+c₂⟩. At t=1, both nonconstant terms are zero, so F(1)=⟨1,1⟩ requires c₁=c₂=1. Thus option a is correct.

after.name: Question 16
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨3(t-1)^{2},\,4{t}^{3}-1⟩\text{d}t
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨3(t-1)^{2},\,4{t}^{3}-1⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int 3(t-1)^{2}\,\text{d}t,\int (4{t}^{3}-1)\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨{(t-1)}^{3}+{c}_{1},\,{t}^{4}-t+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

  

The initial condition $F(1)=⟨1,\,1⟩$ gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1)=⟨{((1)-1)}^{3}+{c}_{1},\,(1)^{4}-(1)+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,1⟩ \\ ⟨{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=1$ and ${c}_{2}=1.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨{(t-1)}^{3}+1,\,{t}^{4}-t+1⟩.
$$

First, we note that

F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨3(t−1)2,4t3−1⟩dt

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

∫⟨3(t−1)2,4t3−1⟩dt=⟨∫3(t−1)2dt,∫(4t3−1)dt⟩=⟨(t−1)3+c1,t4−t+c2⟩.

The initial condition F(1)=⟨1,1⟩ gives F(1)=⟨((1)−1)3+c1,(1)4−(1)+c2⟩=⟨1,1⟩⟨c1,c2⟩=⟨1,1⟩.

Therefore, c1=1 and c2=1. Consequently F(t)=⟨(t−1)3+1,t4−t+1⟩.

Your Answer:
⟨t3+1,t4−t+1⟩

If F′(t)=⟨t+t,2t⟩ and F(1)=⟨2,0⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨4t3/2+3t2+56,2t+ln⁡2⟩
b
⟨3t2+56,2t−2ln⁡2⟩
c
⟨4t3/26,2tln⁡2+ln⁡2⟩
d
⟨4t3/2+56,2tln⁡2⟩
e
⟨4t3/2+3t2+56,2t−2ln⁡2⟩
Submit

decision.explanation: Integrating gives ⟨(2/3)t^(3/2)+t²/2+c₁, 2^t/ln(2)+c₂⟩. The initial condition sets c₁=5/6 and c₂=−2/ln(2), yielding option e.

after.name: Question 17
after.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\sqrt{t}+t,\,{2}^{t}⟩\text{d}t
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\sqrt{t}+t,\,{2}^{t}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int (\sqrt{t}+t)\,\text{d}t,\int {2}^{t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2{t}^{3/2}}{3}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{c}_{1},\,\frac{{2}^{t}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

   

The initial condition $F(1)=⟨2,\,0⟩$ gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1)=⟨\frac{2(1)^{3/2}}{3}+\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+{c}_{1},\,\frac{{2}^{1}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨2,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨\frac{7}{6}+{c}_{1},\,\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨2,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=\frac{5}{6}$ and ${c}_{2}=-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$ Consequently

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =⟨\frac{2{t}^{3/2}}{3}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{5}{6},\,\frac{{2}^{t}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{4{t}^{3/2}+3{t}^{2}+5}{6},\,\frac{{2}^{t}-2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

If F′(t)=⟨t+t,2t⟩ and F(1)=⟨2,0⟩, then F(t)=

a
⟨4t3/2+3t2+56,2t+ln⁡2⟩
b
⟨3t2+56,2t−2ln⁡2⟩

⟨4t3/26,2tln⁡2+ln⁡2⟩

⟨4t3/2+3t2+56,2t−2ln⁡2⟩
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

F(t)=∫F′(t)dt=∫⟨t+t,2t⟩dt

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

∫⟨t+t,2t⟩dt=⟨∫(t+t)dt,∫2tdt⟩=⟨2t3/23+t22+c1,2tln⁡2+c2⟩.

The initial condition F(1)=⟨2,0⟩ gives F(1)=⟨2(1)3/23+122+c1,21ln⁡2+c2⟩=⟨2,0⟩⟨76+c1,2ln⁡2+c2⟩=⟨2,0⟩.

Therefore, c1=56 and c2=−2ln⁡2. Consequently

F(t)=⟨2t3/23+t22+56,2tln⁡2−2ln⁡2⟩=⟨4t3/2+3t2+56,2t−2ln⁡2⟩.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Antiderivative of a Vector-Valued Function That Satisfies a Given Initial Condition
content.worked_solution:
First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\sqrt{t}+t,\,{2}^{t}⟩\text{d}t
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\sqrt{t}+t,\,{2}^{t}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int (\sqrt{t}+t)\,\text{d}t,\int {2}^{t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2{t}^{3/2}}{3}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{c}_{1},\,\frac{{2}^{t}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

   

The initial condition $F(1)=⟨2,\,0⟩$ gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1)=⟨\frac{2(1)^{3/2}}{3}+\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+{c}_{1},\,\frac{{2}^{1}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨2,\,0⟩ \\ ⟨\frac{7}{6}+{c}_{1},\,\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨2,\,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=\frac{5}{6}$ and ${c}_{2}=-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$ Consequently

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =⟨\frac{2{t}^{3/2}}{3}+\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{5}{6},\,\frac{{2}^{t}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{4{t}^{3/2}+3{t}^{2}+5}{6},\,\frac{{2}^{t}-2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨\frac{4}{t+1}\,,3\sqrt{t}⟩\text{d}t.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨\frac{4}{t+1}\,,3\sqrt{t}⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int \frac{4}{t+1}\,\text{d}t,\int 3\sqrt{t}\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨4\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+{c}_{1},\,2{t}^{\frac{3}{2}}+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}

$$
F(t)=⟨4\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+2,\,2{t}^{3/2}-1⟩.

First, we note that 

$$
F(t)=\int {F}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t=\int ⟨-\operatorname{csc}⁡(t)\operatorname{cot}⁡(t)\,,3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)⟩\text{d}t.
$$

To integrate a vector-valued function, we integrate each component separately. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ⟨-\operatorname{csc}⁡(t)\operatorname{cot}⁡(t)\,,3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)⟩\text{d}t & =⟨\int -\operatorname{csc}⁡(t)\operatorname{cot}⁡(t)\,\text{d}t,\int 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\,\text{d}t⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{csc}⁡(t)+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+{c}_{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

The initial condition $F(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨4,\,-2⟩$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}F(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+{c}_{1},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨4,\,-2⟩ \\ ⟨1+{c}_{1},\,-1+{c}_{2}⟩ & =⟨4,\,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${c}_{1}=3$ and ${c}_{2}=-1.$ Consequently

$$
F(t)=⟨\operatorname{csc}⁡(t)+3,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)-1⟩.
$$
